_comment: The Museum encyclopedia's explainers (ui-spec.md component 18, design.md 1.1): how things work, drawn as engineering sheets. Outside the frozen content pack, like strings.json, so text fixes reach running games. Each sheet has a drawing from assets/ui/explainers/ (made by assets-raw/explainers/make_explainer_art.py), three points, an 'In Launch Window' line, and optionally a legend and bars drawn by the client. Every figure is checked (design.md 1.1). No inline bold: a label can't switch fonts mid-text.

explainers.title: Suborbital vs orbital
explainers.summary: Why reaching space is easy and staying up is hard: Newton's cannon, two Mercury flights side by side, and the rocket equation.

sheets.title: Falling around the world

points.title: Space is close
points.text: The edge of space is only about 100 km up: an hour's drive, if you could drive straight up. Reaching it is the easy part. Go up, then fall straight back down. That's a suborbital flight.

points.title: Orbit means falling sideways
points.text: Anything you throw falls back down. Throw it faster and it lands farther away. Throw it fast enough and the ground curves away beneath it as quickly as it falls: it keeps falling, all the way around the Earth. That's an orbit.

points.title: The 8-kilometre rule
points.text: Earth's surface drops away about 5 metres for every 8 km you travel in a straight line. Anything you let go of falls about 5 metres in its first second. So travel 8 km every second, about 28,000 km/h, and you fall exactly as fast as the ground drops away.

sheets.inGame: The goal Human in space needs only a suborbital flight. Human in orbit needs the full 7.8 km/s, and a rocket that can lift your capsule to low Earth orbit.

sheets.title: Height isn't the hard part

points.title: Same capsule, similar height
points.text: In May 1961 a Mercury capsule carried Alan Shepard on a 15-minute suborbital hop. Nine months later the same kind of capsule carried John Glenn three times around the world. Glenn flew only a little higher. Drawn to scale, both flights skim just above the air.

points.title: The difference is speed
points.text: Glenn went about 3.4 times as fast. The energy of motion grows with the square of the speed, so every kilogram of his capsule carried about 12 times as much of it. The rocket had to supply all of it.

points.title: So orbit needs a much bigger rocket
points.text: Shepard's Redstone weighed about 30 tonnes at liftoff. Glenn needed an Atlas of about 120 tonnes, first built as an intercontinental missile. Yuri Gagarin had already orbited in April 1961 on the Soviet R-7, another missile turned launcher.

sheets.inGame: Crewed programs fly a suborbital configuration first, such as Vostok · Suborbital flight. The orbital one needs a stronger human-rated rocket, and its program goal pays twice the prestige.

sheets.title: The rocket's hardest bargain

points.title: Fuel to carry fuel
points.text: A rocket has to lift its own propellant, and the propellant that lifts that. In 1903 Konstantin Tsiolkovsky worked out the result: the propellant needed grows exponentially with the speed you want. Needing about 3.8 times the speed (counting what gravity and air take on the way up) raises the propellant share from 57% to 96%.

points.title: Why rockets come in stages
points.text: Tanks, engines and the crew all have to fit in the last 4%. That's barely possible in one piece, so orbital rockets throw weight away on the way up. Even the Atlas, with steel tank walls thinner than a coin, dropped two of its three main engines.

points.title: Getting home is harder too
points.text: A suborbital capsule falls back by itself. An orbit never ends on its own: a retrorocket must brake the capsule just enough to dip into the air. Then the air turns about 12 times as much energy into heat, and the heat shield has to survive it.

sheets.inGame: In the VAB, compare a rocket's Suborbital payload with its LEO payload: the same rocket lifts far less to orbit. On Vostok · Orbital flight, the Retrofire step is the brake that brings the capsule home.

explainers.title: Rendezvous
explainers.summary: Why a spacecraft brakes to catch up with another, and how crews learned to meet and dock in orbit.

sheets.title: Slow down to catch up

points.title: Lower orbits are faster
points.text: Gravity pulls harder close to the Earth, so a craft in a low orbit has to fly faster to keep falling around it, and it has a shorter way to go. The lower the orbit, the shorter the lap.

points.title: Speed up, and you fall behind
points.text: Fire your engine towards a craft ahead of you and the extra speed lifts you into a higher orbit. A higher orbit takes longer to go round, so the target pulls away. A pilot's instincts, trained in aircraft, say the opposite.

points.title: Brake to catch up
points.text: To close the gap, you brake. The lower, quicker orbit gains a few minutes on every lap. Once you're just below the target, burn forward to rise and match its orbit.

sheets.inGame: Every Retrofire step uses the same idea. Braking lowers the orbit; on the far side of the Earth it dips into the air, and the craft comes home.

sheets.title: Learning to meet in orbit

points.title: Close isn't together
points.text: In August 1962 Vostok 3 and 4 passed within about 6.5 km, but neither could change its orbit, and they drifted apart. In June 1965 Gemini 4 tried to fly up to its own spent upper stage by pointing at it and thrusting. The stage only seemed to slip away, and the crew gave up to save fuel.

points.title: “Dr. Rendezvous”
points.text: In 1963 an Air Force pilot named Buzz Aldrin finished a doctorate at MIT on steering to a rendezvous by eye: hold the target still against the background stars, and correct whenever it drifts. On Gemini 12, in 1966, his radar failed, and he worked the approach out by hand with a sextant and charts.

points.title: Then came docking
points.text: Gemini 6A and 7 met in December 1965 and flew as close as about 30 cm. Gemini 8 made the first docking in March 1966; two uncrewed Soviet craft, Kosmos 186 and 188, docked automatically in 1967. The Moon landings depended on it: the lander had to find its command ship again in lunar orbit.

sheets.inGame: The goal Two crews together asks only for two craft within a few kilometres, which well-timed launches can manage, as Vostok 3 and 4 did. A real rendezvous needs a craft that can change its own orbit.

explainers.title: Going to the Moon
explainers.summary: The trip to the Moon priced in speed changes, and why the rocket that pays for it is so big.

sheets.title: The speed bill for the Moon

points.title: Orbit is halfway
points.text: Reaching low Earth orbit costs about 9.4 km/s of speed change, counting what gravity and air take on the way up. A saying credited to the writer Robert Heinlein puts it neatly: once you're in orbit, you're halfway to anywhere.

points.title: Every stop costs speed
points.text: Leaving Earth orbit for the Moon takes about 3.1 km/s more. The Moon has no air, so slowing into orbit around it, landing, climbing back up and setting off for home must all be done with rockets, and every one of those rockets has to be carried there first.

points.title: The air is free
points.text: The way home is the cheap part. Earth's atmosphere does the braking that would otherwise need another big rocket; a returning crew pays for it with a heat shield and parachutes instead of fuel.

sheets.inGame: In the VAB every rocket lists its payload to TLI, trans-lunar injection: what it can send toward the Moon. Every rocket of the early era reads 0 kg there.

sheets.title: Why the Moon rocket is so big

points.title: Fuel to carry fuel
points.text: Each extra km/s multiplies the size of the rocket instead of adding to it, because the propellant for the last leg has to be lifted by every leg before it. An orbital rocket is already about 96% propellant; for the Moon, its payload is mostly another rocket.

points.title: Split the spacecraft
points.text: Landing one big ship on the Moon and flying it home would have needed an even larger rocket. Apollo landed only a light lander while the command ship waited in lunar orbit, and the two met again before going home. NASA engineer John Houbolt argued hard for this plan, and it fit the whole trip on one Saturn V.

points.title: Big, and still a gamble
points.text: A Saturn V weighed about 2,900 t at liftoff, some 24 times the Atlas that flew America's first orbital missions. The Soviet N1, almost as big, flew four times between 1969 and 1972 and failed every time.

sheets.inGame: Rockets come in classes, and a bigger class needs a higher VAB level before you can open it. Every rocket of the early era is Light.

explainers.title: Restarting an engine in space
explainers.summary: Why lighting a rocket engine after a coast is hard when the propellant floats, and the three ways engineers solved it.

sheets.title: Fuel with no down

points.title: Everything falls together
points.text: While a spacecraft coasts, it and everything inside it are falling at the same rate, so nothing settles. Propellant breaks into floating blobs, creeps along the tank walls and sloshes at the slightest nudge.

points.title: Pumps want liquid, not gas
points.text: A big engine's pumps spin very fast and need a steady column of liquid. A gulp of gas can make them race out of control or starve the engine as it starts. Some engines can be lit only a few times, or only once, so a bad start may be the last chance.

points.title: Nudge, then light
points.text: The cure is a settling burn: small rockets fire for a few seconds to push the craft forward, the propellant drifts back to the bottom of its tanks, and only then does the main engine start. The Saturn V's third stage did this before it relit to leave Earth orbit for the Moon.

sheets.inGame: The R-7 lights every engine on the ground for this reason: in the early 1950s nobody knew whether a big engine could be started reliably high up. Its history note tells the story.

sheets.title: Three ways to a sure restart

points.title: Simple engines restart best
points.text: An engine fed by gas pressure has no pumps to starve, and propellants that ignite the moment they meet need no spark. Apollo's service module engine, which took the crew into lunar orbit and out again, was built this way. So was the lunar module's ascent engine, which had no backup.

points.title: Learned the hard way
points.text: Several of the first Soviet probes to Venus and Mars, in 1961 and 1962, never left Earth orbit: their top stage had to start after a coast in orbit, and it failed. On one, in August 1962, a small settling rocket didn't fire and the stage tumbled. Starting an engine in weightlessness took years of trial and error.

points.title: Every fix has a price
points.text: Self-igniting propellants are poisonous and attack seals. Gas-fed engines need heavy, thick-walled tanks. Bags and screens add weight and can wear out. Engineers pick the trade that fits: the more an engine must restart, the simpler it is built.

sheets.inGame: Retrofire is a start in space too, and Vostok's single retrorocket can't be fired twice. A step's odds rest on the reliability of the parts it uses; Payload R&D in the SET Centre raises it.

explainers.title: Hypergolics and steering jets
explainers.summary: Propellants that light the moment they touch, and the small jets that turn, slide and stop a spacecraft.

sheets.title: Fuels that light themselves

points.title: Two liquids, one flame
points.text: Hypergolic means a fuel and an oxidiser that burst into flame the instant they touch: no spark, no igniter, nothing to fail. Open two valves and the engine runs; close them and it stops. The word was coined by German rocket chemists in the 1940s.

points.title: Ready to wait
points.text: Liquid oxygen boils at −183 °C and must be topped up until the last minutes before launch. A hypergolic pair stays liquid at room temperature for months, so a missile can stand ready in its silo, and a spacecraft can wait days in orbit before its next burn.

points.title: The price is poison
points.text: The usual pair, a hydrazine fuel with nitrogen tetroxide, is toxic and eats through seals, so ground crews load it in sealed suits. In October 1960 an R-16 missile, fuelled with a similar self-igniting pair, exploded on its pad at Baikonur and killed at least 78 people.

sheets.inGame: Every rocket of the early era burns liquid oxygen in its main stages, so each one is fuelled on launch day, and the Countdown step can still hold. Self-lighting propellants arrive with later rockets and spacecraft.

sheets.title: Steering with small jets

points.title: Push one way, move the other
points.text: With no air there are no wings or fins to steer with. A reaction control system is a set of small rocket jets around the craft, usually grouped in fours. Each jet pushes the craft the opposite way to its exhaust.

points.title: Short, sharp and many
points.text: Steering jets fire in bursts of a fraction of a second, thousands of times on one flight. Self-lighting propellants suit them: there's nothing to ignite, only valves to open. The first capsules used simpler stuff: Vostok puffed cold nitrogen gas, Mercury broke down hydrogen peroxide.

points.title: Gemini 8's spin
points.text: In March 1966, just after the first docking, a jet on Gemini 8 stuck open. After undocking the capsule spun faster and faster, up to about one turn a second. Neil Armstrong shut the jets down and stopped the spin with the separate re-entry jets. Once those were used, the rules said come home, so the flight ended early.

sheets.inGame: The Reentry preparations step is steering-jet work: turning the capsule so its retrorockets point forward. On Faith 7, Gordon Cooper did it by hand, lining up on marks drawn on his window.
